newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin dairy farmer leads symbolic milk strike.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin dairy farmer leads symbolic milk strike.

text.p: A Wisconsin dairy farmer angered by the sharp drop in milk prices late last year claimed Wednesday that 10,000 of his fellow producers had joined him in a one-day strike.

The largely symbolic strike -- there are 26,000 dairy farmers in Wisconsin alone -- aimed to attract attention to what farmer Darin Von Ruden of Westby, Wis., said were irresponsible federal government milk pricing policies.
"If the government wants a free market, then there has to be a free market all the way from the milk producer to the consumer," Von Ruden said.
He complained that large dairy product manufacturers take advantage of an arcane government pricing system to manipulate the price of milk.
Von Ruden said farmers from Wisconsin, Minnesota, Texas, Vermont, New York, and Pennsylvania had contacted him saying they would join the strike.
Other industry sources doubted that many farmers would join the strike and said milk supplies would be unaffected.
About half the nation's milk production is used to make cheese.
Consumers have been paying relatively high prices for milk since a price spike last summer caused by shortages of feedgrains, which put a pinch on dairy farmers.
For a while farmers benefited and were paid record-high wholesale prices of up to $17 per 100 pounds for their milk.

But that changed suddenly in late October, when a 25 percent drop in cheese prices at the obscure National Cheese Exchange in Green Bay, Wis., drove wholesale milk prices down closer to their historical average of $12.50 per 100 pounds.

Von Ruden said consumers were still paying a retail milk price that should translate to $30 per 100 pounds to farmers, and he suggested a $15 government floor. Current law calls for a phasing out of federal milk price supports of $11.15 per 100 pounds by the end of the decade.

Supporters of the dairy farmers complain that cheese prices at the Green Bay exchange -- which holds one weekly half-hour cheese trading session each Friday morning -- are manipulated by large dairy product firms and do not reflect the actual supply and demand for milk and cheese.
The cheese price set at the exchange is the driving force behind milk prices and is a key ingredient in the federal milk pricing formula.

"In general over the long term, the (exchange) price reflects supply and demand. But the government (milk) pricing structure does have a distorting influence," said Paul Zimmerman, a lobbyist with the Wisconsin Farm Bureau Federation.
A report last year on the cheese exchange by University of Wisconsin researchers in Madison cited possible instances of price manipulation that may have hurt farmers.

The Wisconsin state legislature is currently debating a bill that would regulate the exchange by making it illegal to make off-exchange cheese purchases at prices that differ from those on the exchange.
The cheese exchange is seen as a market of last resort, and roughly 1 percent of the 6 billion pounds of cheese produced annually in the United States changes hands there.
